Key Findings

Districts need to see impact on diagnostic test scores.
The ESSA Level III study, the end-of-program reviews and the published district results all measure growth on Paper’s outcome measures. Districts and RFP evaluators want to see evidence that GROW moves diagnostic test scores.
Developing systems for obtaining diagnostic data comes first.
Getting data flowing is key to reporting what matters most to district leaders.
Session transcripts are a resource for improving implementation measurement.
Every session records attendance, attentiveness, talk time, exit tickets, a student survey and a full transcript. Other indicators of delivery quality could be developed from transcripts.
Improvements to district reporting could have an outsized impact.
Reports that show growth on diagnostic measures, more fine-grained measures of implementation, and associations between implementation quality and outcomes will tell a fuller story for districts evaluating the return on their investment.

About Paper

Paper has provided tutoring to K–12 districts since 2014. This assessment covers GROW, its live, small-group high-impact tutoring program, which districts buy as a Tier 2 intervention in reading and math. It covers GROW as delivered to district partners across grades and terms, with grades 3–8 during the school day as the main focus. It excludes Sprout, Paper's AI tutor, and Paper's on-demand tutoring and writing-feedback products.

The Impact Process Model

The figure below maps how GROW is intended to produce learning gains: from program design, through tutor practice, student participation and student experience, to learning outcomes, with the two feedback loops that carry results back to districts. Solid boxes mark elements that data or direct observation show are happening. Dashed boxes mark elements Paper describes but has not yet shown with data, including well-defined elements that are not yet measured. Tags apply to boxes, not arrows; the figure does not claim that any element causes the next. Numbered markers point to the open questions listed beneath it.

ℹ️ Click any column for model detail and its open question. Switch on the measurement layer to see where each priority (P1–P4) applies, and click a badge for detail.

Model Description

ElementDescription
ContextTier 2 support for students who need it most, selected by test scores or by teacher and district judgment depending on the district. Delivered live by video, usually during the school day. At roughly $1,500 per student a year, districts expect to see gains on their diagnostic benchmarks.
Program DesignLevel-matched groups of three, placed by pretest, following a scope and sequence agreed with the district. Tutors are W-2 employees with about 150 hours of training before their first lesson, and the same tutor stays with a group for the cycle, at about 90 minutes a week. The NSSA badge certifies this design; delivery against it is not yet documented, so these boxes are dashed.
Tutor PracticeInstruction and feedback at each student's level, which Paper regards as the active ingredient, delivered through a Gradual Release structure (I do, we do, you do) with enough challenge that students work things out without giving up. Every session is transcribed, but the transcripts have not yet been analyzed.
Student ParticipationAttendance (60–81% in recent reviews, against a 70% benchmark) and active participation: attentiveness, talk time and chat. Both are measured in every session.
Student ExperienceWhether students understood the lesson is asked in the survey after every session, alongside a tutor rating (4.6 of 5 in a recent district review). Feeling known by the tutor and being productively challenged are part of the design but are not yet asked.
Learning OutcomesMastery of taught standards is measured by exit tickets and GROW's pre- and post-assessments. Growth on diagnostic benchmarks (i-Ready, MAP, AIMSweb), the outcome districts weigh most, is measured only where districts share data. State test gains are a longer-term goal for long-tenured districts.
Feedback LoopsThe mid-program review shows each district its implementation data against GROW targets and lists standards for teachers to reinforce. The end-of-program review, together with teachers' sense of value, informs renewal. Both reviews are delivered on schedule; how districts act on them is not yet documented.

Evidence Landscape

Before identifying measurement opportunities, it is worth cataloging the evidence Paper already has. This inventory is what lets the measurement priorities read as gap-filling rather than as starting from zero.

Evidence AssetWhat It ShowsLimitations
ESSA Level III study (2025)SourceInstructure and International Centre for EdTech Impact; commissioned by Paper
 Among 123 students in grades 4, 6, 7 and 8 math, higher attendance was associated with higher end-of-program scores in grades 7–8. Correlational, no comparison group; outcome is GROW's own assessment; no relationship found in grades 4 and 6; one subject.
NSSA Tutoring Program Design badgeSourceNational Student Support Accelerator, Stanford
 GROW's documented design meets research-based standards for high-impact tutoring, including tutor consistency, dosage and alignment. Certifies design, not delivery or effectiveness.
District end-of-program reviewsSourcePaper; e.g., summer 2026, grades 6–8 math, 143 students
 Gains on GROW's pre- and post-assessments (+19 points among students with both scores), and larger gains among students attending 80% or more of sessions. Internal measures only; about half the cohort completed both assessments; no comparison group.
Session-level implementation and survey dataSourcePaper platform, every session
 Attendance, attentiveness, talk time, exit-ticket results and post-session ratings for every student and session. Measures how much and how attentively students took part, not instructional quality; only exit tickets and attendance have been linked to gains, in an earlier, small analysis.
Full session transcriptsSourcePaper platform, every session
 A complete record of what tutors and students said in every session. Not yet analyzed.
Published district resultsSourcepaper.co partner stories
 Pre/post gains on i-Ready and other benchmarks in several districts; one, in grade 5 math with 40 students, compares GROW students with non-participants (+9 vs. +5 scale points). Mostly pre/post, reported as relative percentages; designs and samples are not stated alongside the results.
Tier 2 matched-comparison study (in progress)SourcePaper, run in-house; about 7 districts
 Will estimate GROW's effect on i-Ready, MAP and AIMSweb against matched non-participants in grades 3–8, reading and math separately. Not yet complete; draws on districts that share data and have stayed with Paper.
Randomized trials (in progress)SourceStanford
 Will provide the strongest causal evidence on GROW. Results about a year away.
Research on high-impact tutoringSourceMeta-analyses and trials, e.g., Nickow et al. 2020; Kraft, Schueler & Falken 2024
 School-day, small-group tutoring with consistent, trained tutors produces meaningful gains; virtual programs average smaller effects. Not specific to GROW. The closest virtual analogue found negative reading effects where dose was low and tutors rotated, features GROW is designed to avoid.

Three patterns stand out. First, Paper's implementation record reflects a strong start point: every session produces attendance, engagement, exit-ticket and survey data, plus a full transcript. Second, every outcome result is measured on GROW's own assessments, which districts and RFP evaluators discount. Third, causal impact studies that will show whether GROW works are under way and in capable hands. What sits between them is routine, district-by-district evidence on the measures districts already trust, and that depends first on diagnostic data. In addition, improving measurement of implementation quality and routinely testing associations between implementation and outcomes would provide valuable data that may uncover patterns not visible from overall “effects”. It is not clear that a focused effort on building and routinely using implementation measurement in this way is a priority.

Cobalt also reviewed the published research behind each element of the model. That review is summarized in the evidence review appendix.

Impact Measurement Opportunities

Paper's measurement challenge is less about what to measure than about access. Its platform already records what happens in every session; what it cannot yet do routinely is connect that record to the diagnostic scores districts use to judge GROW. For an intervention that costs about $1,500 per student a year, districts give gains on internal assessments little weight.

That makes sequence matter more than volume. Diagnostic data has to flow before Paper can test how its own measures relate to it, and both have to be in place before district reports can carry the evidence renewal conversations need. The causal studies already under way, the Tier 2 study run in-house and the Stanford randomized trials, are a priority for Paper but are well staffed and do not need outside support now, so they appear here as evidence assets rather than as priorities.

We therefore organize the assessment into one track of four priorities: Priorities 1 and 2 build the foundation: getting diagnostic data flowing, and establishing how GROW's internal measures relate to it. Both can begin now. Priority 3 adds measures of session quality drawn from transcripts and surveys Paper already collects, and Priority 4 turns all of this into the district report. Each priority states the value Paper itself places on it.

The Four Priorities

The four priorities can each be commissioned on its own. Priority 1 is operational, Priority 2 analytic, Priority 3 runs on transcripts and surveys rather than scores and serves Paper's own tutor coaching as much as districts, and Priority 4 is a reporting build that draws on all three. Combining them would hide those differences; splitting them further would promote sub-steps to priorities. The order follows dependency: the report comes last because it draws on the other three, though it does not need to wait for all of them.

Measurement Focus Which audience each priority serves Districts RFP Account teams Product
● Primary driver    ○ Contributing factor    – Not applicable
1 Get diagnostic data flowing, and know whether it is Now ● ● ● ○ ▼
Operational

Paper's contracts already include data-sharing clauses, i-Ready data arrives automatically from some districts through Curriculum Associates, and a new process launching this month raises data sharing at kickoff and connects Paper directly with each district's data lead. The target is clear: 60% or more of medium-to-large districts sharing diagnostics within six to eight months.

Value to Paper: Essential. District reports, renewal conversations and claims drawn from pooled data all wait on this.

What to measure

  • Share of districts sending diagnostic data, by district size and contract stage, against the 60% target
  • Time from contract signature to first usable data file
  • Where requests stall: kickoff, data-lead contact, file transfer or format
  • Whether Clever or ClassLink can deliver i-Ready, MAP and AIMSweb scores for districts that authorize it, confirmed with both vendors

Paper's own diagnosis is that district motivation is too low and friction too high, so track both: districts that agree but never send, and districts that never agree. They need different fixes.

2 Link GROW's measures to the diagnostics districts trust As Tier 2 data arrive ● ○ ○ ● ▼
Analytic

Exit tickets, pre- and post-assessments and attendance tell Paper a great deal about each cycle, but districts will weigh them only once they know how those measures relate to i-Ready or MAP. The Tier 2 dataset will be the first place Paper holds internal and diagnostic scores for the same students across several districts, which makes estimating that relationship nearly free. Start there, then refresh the estimates as Priority 1 brings in more districts.

Value to Paper: High. It decides how much weight GROW's internal measures can carry in district reports, and it supplies the pooled estimates behind claims about what a district's implementation quality would be expected to produce.

What to measure

  • How closely GROW pre/post gains and exit-ticket mastery track diagnostic growth for the same students, by grade and subject
  • Which implementation measures (attendance, sessions received, tutor continuity, exit-ticket performance) predict diagnostic growth
  • Whether those relationships hold across districts that select students differently
  • Expected diagnostic growth at given levels of implementation, for use in district reports

Confirm that the Tier 2 data use agreements permit this analysis before planning on it. Districts that share data and stay are likely stronger implementers than those that leave, so state which kinds of district each estimate represents.

3 Session quality from transcripts As capacity allows ○ – ○ ● ▼
Internal

Every GROW session is transcribed, so Paper already holds a complete record of what tutors and students say. One or two measures of tutor behavior corresponding to Paper’s theory of instructional quality (such as whether tutors give feedback at each student's level) and of student responses (such as whether students explain their reasoning), would show districts that sessions are active instruction, sharpen the analysis of districts with modest results in Priority 4, and give Paper a basis for coaching tutors. Adapting the engagement measures Paper is building for Sprout, licensing existing discourse metrics, or a graduate-student project are all plausible routes.

A cheaper first step needs no transcripts: add two items to the survey students already complete after every session, one on feeling challenged and one on connection to the tutor. Feeling challenged is a practical stand-in for productive struggle; the evidence suggests connection to the tutor matters mainly as a lever for attendance.

Value to Paper: Paper regards evidence of session quality as far less persuasive to districts than outcome effects, but it may be worth pursuing.

What to measure

  • Key tutor-practice measures, such as feedback matched to the student's level or the balance of guiding questions to direct answers
  • Key student-response measures, such as how often students explain their reasoning
  • Two items added to the post-session survey students already complete: whether they felt challenged, and whether they feel connected to their tutor
  • Whether any of these measures predicts exit-ticket and diagnostic growth beyond attendance

Check any automated score against a sample of human-coded sessions before it appears in a district report.

4 A next-generation district evidence report Spring 2027 renewals ● – ● ○ ▼
Reporting

Paper's mid- and end-of-program reviews already reach every district on schedule, are generated automatically, and are being enriched with what account teams know about each district. The next version would put diagnostic results in front of district leaders, replace the single 80% attendance split with better measures of implementation (mid-year) and associations between implementation and growth (end-of-year), and give account teams a credible story for what Paper calls red districts, those with its weakest results: for whom GROW worked, under what conditions, and what would raise the rest.

A district with poor overall results can still re-sign on strong gains in the standards it cares about most, and the report should be built to find them. Fixing the analyses in the template, rather than choosing them district by district, also settles the pull between full transparency and a sales-friendly story.

The red-district analysis does not have to wait for diagnostic data: Paper already holds platform data and internal outcomes for past red districts, and a study of which implementation patterns separate students who gained from those who did not could start now, possibly as a Stanford graduate-student project. The report can launch with the measures that exist today and add others, including the session-quality indicators from Priority 3, as they become available.

Value to Paper: High, and the most natural candidate for a focused build with outside support. This is where Priorities 1 - 3 reach districts.

What to measure

  • Diagnostic growth for participating students, with whatever comparison the data allow
  • Summary of implementation quality using traditional and newly derived (see Priority 3) metrics.
  • Implementation analyses: growth by sessions received, attendance, tutoring quality, and student engagement.
  • Assessment completion across the full cohort, so results describe all participants
  • Teachers' judgment of value and student survey results

Set implementation targets in the mid-program review only where analysis shows they predict growth. Attendance and exit-ticket performance qualify today; other targets should earn their place the same way.

What Changes If You Do This

Today, a district leader asking whether GROW worked for her students gets an answer in GROW's own assessments which leaves open the question of impact on diagnostic test scores. With these four priorities in place, Paper can credibly report diagnostic test score growth, implementation quality, association between implementation quality and test scores. Paper's pooled data may be able to predict for a district what the impact of attendance, dosage and quality will be on students . For a district with modest results, the same report shows which students and schools gained and what would raise the rest, so renewal turns on improving implementation rather than on whether to cancel. And account teams can tell that story in every district, on schedule.

About This Report

This report has two purposes: first, to articulate a working model of the mechanisms through which GROW is intended to produce impact; and second, to identify where measurement would most improve Paper's ability to understand and demonstrate that impact. It is an assessment, not an evaluation.

  1. Articulate a working model of how GROW is intended to produce impact, from program design through tutor practice and student participation to learning outcomes.
  2. Use that model to identify and prioritize opportunities for impact measurement.

Our aim is to describe impact measurement opportunities that would advance Paper’s strategic goal of being able to credibly demonstrate impact to each district partner. These opportunities are complementary to ongoing causal impact studies, including a planned Tier II QED and RCTs being run at Stanford.
